intro: Ordered practice ladders built from the AtCoder Categories problem tags. Each ladder walks one technique from its easiest AtCoder appearance to its hardest, picked so that every rung introduces a model the previous rungs did not cover — rather than ten variations of the same idea. Difficulty numbers are AtCoder's own estimated difficulty, coloured by the standard rating bands.
how_to_use: Sit with a rung for 30–45 minutes before opening anything. The "nudge" under each problem is the one idea the problem turns on, not a solution — read it only when you are genuinely stuck, and read the editorial after you have solved it either way. If a rung takes more than two sittings, drop back and do a second problem in the same model before continuing.

ladders.name: Tree DP
ladders.blurb: Twenty problems out of the 102 tagged Tree DP, from 704 to 2920. The progression is deliberate: one DFS returning one number, then a returned state, then rerooting, then the knapsack merge, then a DP with something wrapped around it, and finally the named machinery (Steiner trees, virtual trees, dynamic tree DP) that shows up in ARC/AGC.

tiers.name: Foundations
tiers.note: One DFS, one value per subtree. The goal here is to stop thinking about the tree and start thinking about what a child hands back to its parent.

problems.label: ABC 333 D
problems.title: Erase Leaves
problems.teaches: The single most reused primitive: root the tree, compute size[v] in one post-order pass.
problems.nudge: Root at vertex 1. Each neighbour of the root heads an independent subtree, and you must delete every one of them except the largest.

problems.label: ABC 348 E
problems.title: Minimize Sum of Distances
problems.teaches: The canonical introduction to rerooting: compute the answer at the root, then slide it to every other vertex in O(1) per edge.
problems.nudge: Get f(1) = sum of C_i * dist(1,i) with one DFS. Moving the root across edge (u,v) changes it by `total weight - 2 * (subtree weight of v)`.

problems.label: ABC 397 E
problems.title: Path Decomposition of a Tree
problems.teaches: A child hands back more than a number — here it hands back how many loose path-ends it still has. Feasibility DP rather than optimisation.
problems.nudge: Any vertex with three or more children still needing to extend a path is immediately impossible. Track the count of dangling ends and close them greedily as you unwind.

problems.label: ABC 222 E
problems.title: Red and Blue Tree
problems.teaches: Reducing a tree problem to a sequence problem. Half the difficulty of tree DP is spotting when the tree stops mattering.
problems.nudge: Walk the given route once and count how many times each edge is traversed. What remains is a subset-sum over those counts hitting a fixed target.

problems.label: ABC 394 F
problems.title: Alkane
problems.teaches: Merging children is not always a knapsack — often you just sort their values and take the top few. Learn to recognise that shape.
problems.nudge: Every internal vertex needs exactly four incident edges, so dp[v] keeps the best chain downward and you sum the three largest positive child contributions.

tiers.name: Core patterns
tiers.note: The workhorses: counting with subtree sizes, rerooting a non-trivial state, and the tree knapsack. Almost every harder problem is one of these wearing a costume.

problems.label: ABC 312 G
problems.title: Avoid Straight Line
problems.teaches: Counting triples on a tree by fixing the meeting vertex — and by counting the bad cases instead of the good ones.
problems.nudge: Total triples minus the collinear ones. For each vertex, the paths through it split the rest of the tree into its child subtrees plus everything above it.

problems.label: ABC 222 F
problems.title: Expensive Expense
problems.teaches: The same rerooting machinery, but max instead of sum — so you need the best and second-best child in order to exclude the one you came from.
problems.nudge: Keep the top two downward values at each vertex; when descending into child c, pass down the best value that is not c's own.

problems.label: ABC 259 F
problems.title: Select Edges
problems.teaches: Two states per vertex — edge to parent used or not — with a degree cap that turns the merge into a sort-and-take.
problems.nudge: dp[v][0/1] = best weight in v's subtree. For each child, taking its edge gains `w + dp[c][0] - dp[c][1]`; keep the positive gains, sort, take as many as the degree limit allows.

problems.label: ABC 287 F
problems.title: Components
problems.teaches: The O(n^2) subtree knapsack, and the amortisation argument that proves it is quadratic and not cubic. Non-negotiable to know.
problems.nudge: dp[v][k][0/1] = ways to get k components in v's subtree, with v chosen or not. Merge children one at a time, looping only up to the sizes already accumulated.

problems.label: ABC 369 G
problems.title: As far as possible
problems.teaches: Decompose the tree into vertex-disjoint downward chains; answering for every K at once falls out of sorting the chain lengths.
problems.nudge: Each vertex keeps its deepest downward path and the leftover branches become separate chains. Sort all chain lengths descending — the answer for K is a prefix sum.

tiers.name: An outer loop around the DP
tiers.note: The DP is no longer the whole solution. Here it sits inside a binary search, a game-theoretic argument, a rerooting of a two-state DP, or a compressed tree.

problems.label: ABC 218 G
problems.title: Game on Tree 2
problems.teaches: Game DP where the optimising player alternates by depth, plus maintaining a running median down the DFS path.
problems.nudge: Leaves are terminal; internal vertices take max or min of their children by parity. Keep the median of the root-to-current path with two heaps, pushing on entry and popping on exit.

problems.label: ABC 246 G
problems.title: Game on Tree 3
problems.teaches: Parametric search: guess the answer X, rewrite the problem as a boolean, and let a much simpler DP decide it.
problems.nudge: Fix X and mark vertices with value >= X as dangerous. dp[v] = how many dangerous vertices in v's subtree cannot be erased in time; monotone in X, so binary search.

problems.label: ABC 223 G
problems.title: Vertex Deletion
problems.teaches: Rerooting where the state is itself a DP (maximum matching), not just a number. The real test of whether you understand rerooting.
problems.nudge: dp[v][0/1] = matching size in v's subtree with v unmatched / matched. A vertex is removable iff the whole tree keeps the same maximum matching without it — reroot to test all n at once.

problems.label: ABC 207 F
problems.title: Tree Patrolling
problems.teaches: The classic dominating-set state set — chosen / covered by a child / not yet covered — used for counting rather than minimising.
problems.nudge: dp[v][0] = v not covered, [1] = v covered by a child's guard, [2] = guard on v. Merge children as a convolution over the number of covered vertices.

problems.label: ABC 340 G
problems.title: Leaf Color
problems.teaches: When a DP has to run once per colour, build the compressed tree over just that colour's vertices. Total size stays O(n log n).
problems.nudge: Sort a colour's vertices by DFS order, add pairwise LCAs, rebuild the edges with a stack. Then count connected subtrees whose leaf set is exactly that colour.

problems.label: ARC 130 D
problems.title: Zigzag Tree
problems.teaches: A naive child merge is quadratic per vertex here. Rewriting it as cumulative sums is the standard rescue for rank-indexed tree DP.
problems.nudge: dp[v][i] = ways in which v is the i-th smallest among v and its used children. Merging with binomials plus prefix sums keeps the whole thing quadratic overall.

tiers.name: Advanced machinery
tiers.note: Named techniques worth reusing for years: Steiner trees, inclusion–exclusion over a knapsack, multi-dimensional traversal states, and a DP that has to survive updates.

problems.label: ABC 364 G
problems.title: Last Major City
problems.teaches: Bitmask over terminals times vertices, with the two transitions — subset split and edge relax — that define the Steiner tree DP.
problems.nudge: dp[S][v] = cheapest tree connecting terminal set S and containing v. Split S into two halves at v, then relax over edges with Dijkstra for each fixed S.

problems.label: ARC 121 E
problems.title: Directed Tree
problems.teaches: Counting permutations with forbidden positions: count arrangements with at least k bad pairs via a tree knapsack, then alternate signs.
problems.nudge: f[k] = ways to choose k disjoint ancestor–descendant pairs, which is a subtree knapsack. The answer is the alternating sum of f[k] * (n-k)!.

problems.label: ARC 179 D
problems.title: Portable Gate
problems.teaches: Traversal DP where the state carries both a budget and whether you come back to the vertex. The dimension people forget to add.
problems.nudge: dp[v][k][0/1] over v's subtree, k = gate uses, last flag = whether the walk returns to v. Merge children like a knapsack, allowing exactly one non-returning branch.

problems.label: ABC 351 G
problems.title: Hash on Tree
problems.teaches: The DP has to survive point updates. Express each vertex's transition as an affine map and hang it off a heavy-light decomposition.
problems.nudge: dp[v] = A[v] + X[v] * (product of dp over children). Linearise along heavy paths, keep the light-child products aside, and put a segment tree of composed affine maps on each path.
